body: From looking at https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/14997, I want to clarify that purpose of this PR is to allow the alpha to be set to the greyscale value of the RGB channels?

@allenwp the main goal, yes. Main use case is colored particle sheets with no separate alpha channel (similarly to the former proposal), but it also can be used for other remapping features as a side effect.

> @allenwp the main goal, yes. Main use case is colored particle sheets with no separate alpha channel (similarly to the former proposal), but it also can be used for other remapping features as a side effect.

In this case, the well-accepted general purpose approach to generating a greyscale version of a colour image is to use the [luminance](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_color.html#class-color-method-get-luminance) of the colour. By using the average of red, green, and blue channels, you will get a result that produces greens that appear too dark and blues that appear too bright. Using the luminance resolves this issues and produces a greyscale with appropriate apparent brightness for all colours.

When calculating the luminance of a colour, there are a few things to keep in mind:
1. RGB values must be linear-encoded before applying the luminance function (cannot be sRGB encoded, for example)
2. The luminance weights of the luminance function must match the colour primaries used by the red, green, and blue colour channels. These are often the Rec. 709 primaries, but image formats can use other colour primaries. To handle other primaries, you may use the luminance weights of those primaries, but it may be easier to first convert to Rec. 709 primaries (since Godot uses these primaries for all internal rendering).
3. I'm not sure how negative RGB values (out of gamut colours) should be handled, but these might need to be clipped to non-negative in the Rec. 709 gamut before calculating luminance. I can do the math on this at some point before this is merged.

All that said... I'm not actually sure you want the greyscale version of an image for your use-case? I'm having a hard time understanding how this approach would really work well in a general case. For example, using the "RGB Average" approach: a saturated red, green, or blue colour would end up with a low alpha, while a desaturated colour would end up with high alpha, even if these two colours appear similarly bright.

So I'm not sure if either the approach of greyscale or RGB average would be effective as a general approach to generating an alpha value for the purposes of transparency.

Maybe what you want instead would be: `max(red, green, blue)`?

> 0.299R + 0.587G + 0.114B

These are the luminance weights for the old NTSC/PAL standards and should never be used today. I will be creating a PR in the future to update these to the Rec. 709 luminance weights ( 0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B).

> But you've also got a very good point with `max` - maybe we could add "Max RGB" (as you stated) and "Luminance" (with the weighted formula from above) to the remap options then?

It is of utmost importance that new features (even if small) that are added to Godot [solve real-world problems that many users encounter](https://contributing.godotengine.org/en/latest/engine/guidelines/best_practices.html).

So I don't think there is value in adding both until we have a solid use case that both are relevant to a large number of users for specific and real use-cases. Also, as demonstrated by my notes, there is some very real nuance and complexity to adding luminance/greyscale, so it would be better to avoid that complexity altogether if there isn't a strong usecase for it that can't be simply solved by external art tools.

I'm not entirely sure if your use-case justifies adding the new remap option simply because I'm not sure how many users would actually use this in practice, but a `max(r, g, b)` does sound a lot simpler.

If we do add a "Max RGB" remap option, there is the colour channel encoding that's worth considering... I think most users would want this to be sRGB-encoded for a somewhat perceptually uniform value. But I'm not sure exactly how to handle this for HDR formats. So it might be best to keep the encoding "as-is" where SDR images produce sRGB-encoded colour and HDR formats produce linear-encoded colour. In this case, I think it may be as simple as the math operation of `max(r, max(g, b))`??

>These are the luminance weights for the old NTSC/PAL standards and should never be used today. 

true. I also see that we indeed have `color.get_luminance()` that already uses Rec. 709 ones. It's even better then, just `dst[i] = src.get_luminance();` instead of any formulas.

>It is of utmost importance that new features (even if small) that are added to Godot [solve real-world problems that many users encounter](https://contributing.godotengine.org/en/latest/engine/guidelines/best_practices.html). So I don't think there is value in adding both until we have a solid use case that both are relevant to a large number of users for specific and real use-cases.

I mean, the real-use case definitely exists, it's basically the subject of the proposal (i.e. allow automatically deriving the alpha value for an image from the greyscale-ish version of the image for e.g. particles based on sprite sheet, similarly to how Unity allows it). It's the _implementation_ that is indeed problematic here, because there ain't a single definition of what is the "greyscale version of the image" actually is. I've amended the proposal with additional details regarding this.

>Also, as demonstrated by my notes, there is some very real nuance and complexity to adding luminance/greyscale, so it would be better to avoid that complexity altogether if there isn't a strong usecase for it that can't be simply solved by external art tools.

I'm not saying those are straightforward; I do agree there's a lot of possible bikeshedding here. Still, it's not that by providing an option anyone is being _forced_ to use that option; countably how many documented situations do you have of people requiring the particular remapping options that we have now, e.g. inverting channels other than G, or explicitly 1-ing the channel? I do believe those would be used very rarely. I'd even go a step further, and say that because the remapper is still relatively new and wasn't a hugely requested feature AFAIK, it itself would fail the "usecase (...) that can't be simply solved by external art tools". Yet it's been shipped, and I'm really glad it was, because it's a really useful feature.

>If we do add a "Max RGB" remap option, there is the colour channel encoding that's worth considering... I think most users would want this to be sRGB-encoded for a somewhat perceptually uniform value. But I'm not sure exactly how to handle this for HDR formats. So it might be best to keep the encoding "as-is" where SDR images produce sRGB-encoded colour and HDR formats produce linear-encoded colour. In this case, I think it may be as simple as the math operation of max(r, max(g, b))??

Hmm. Come to think about HDR, I assume everyone expects ~alpha~ transparency to be in the [0,1] range, so wouldn't it be `min(max(r,g,b),1)` instead? I don't know if alpha is clamped somewhere later in the remapping code, but I wouldn't assume so.

When used for transparency, it's typical to expect alpha in the [0,1] range to represent 0% through to 100%. But alpha isn't specific to transparency and is just data, so it shouldn't ever be clamped.

Personally, I think using `dst[i] = src.get_luminance();` and consequently changing the remap name to either `Grayscale` or `Luminance` would be the way to go. 
I'm still going to try comparing the different ways of deriving grayscale from color, but I cannot think of many use cases where `max` or `average` would be more useful for color data. For non-color data I don't think getting the luminance is a common use case.

@BlueCube3310 I'll change this to a luminance option then, I'll name it just "Luminance" as per POLA, and arguably it'll be just a luminance remap option, to be used as the user desires. The resulting possibility of "Luminance to alpha" is not that rare of a use case TBH, https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/luminancetoalpha() https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/direct2d/luminance-to-alpha https://www.reddit.com/r/Maya/comments/obce9r/can_anybody_explain_what_does_alpha_to_luminance/ etc. (i.e. many mainstream tools provide explicitly that option)

Here's an image that can be used to test the greyscale/luminance behaviour: [greyscale-test-images.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29181041/greyscale-test-images.zip) Original image | Correct Greyscale | Incorrect Greyscale | Incorrect Greyscale (alternative) --|--|--|-- || | And here's the project (with HDR 2D enabled) that I used to create these: [greyscale_test.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29181141/greyscale_test.zip) **Edit:** Just did a quick test with the current state of this PR using the PNG file I shared. When placing a sprite with luminance mapped to R, G, and B, I get something that looks like the "Incorrect Greyscale (alternative)" example I shared: MRP: [greyscale-simple-test.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29181927/greyscale-simple-test.zip) Generally speaking, I believe that Godot mostly just treats textures as data when importing them. For the most part, it's up to the engine and the rest of the game to interpret that texture data correctly. This means that it's not really possible with the way Godot is currently set up to perform interpretation during the import phase where channel remapping happens. Colour _interpretation_ is required to correctly determine [relative] luminance and a greyscale interpretation of the image. So all that to say, the simple math of `max(r, g, b)` might be the only option without some bigger changes to the way Godot works... And before we merge the addition of `max(r, g, b)`, we will need to wait a while to hear from other users if this is something they need to solve specific problems in their projects... But again, I'm no import expert! Maybe there is some way to correctly interpret colour encoding in a foolproof way.

@allenwp I would reiterate what I said: it's not "incorrect" greyscale per se, because how GS is interpreted wildly differs between tools. XnView MP, Image -> Change color depth -> Greyscale 256 Aseprite v1.3, Sprite -> Color mode -> Greyscale Photopea, Image -> Adjustment -> Desaturate Krita has a tool allowing to select the type of desaturation, and TBH, `max` does a really bad job; for an image like this, it wouldn't really be worth it. Lightness and `avg` are a bit strange, but definitely usable. Both Rec. 709 and Rec. 601 are certainly good, and frankly Rec. 601 looks better for me than Rec. 709 - while there is definitely a lack of more bright areas, the low and middle greys are shaded better. It obviously depends on the particular screen one uses, and then on brightness/contrast/black settings one has. Still, I compared the result from this PR, and I would definitely say it's "close enough" as the greyscale interpretation of the source image to be usable without any problems. It doesn't have to be "perfect" in any way IMVHO, because there is no "perfect" greyscale definition, neither in theory nor practice, and being "good enough" (i.e. usable for practical reasons, e.g. to create particle sheet transparency on-the-fly as in this particular case) is the goal for all graphical tools I know of. **That said,** I'll try tweaking the code to produce the "perfect" result. Shouldn't be hard to do simple ifology there.

It’s true there are a number of approaches to interpreting greyscale from colour, but when using luminance weights to determine the greyscale there is only one correct way to use those luminance weights: applying them to linear-encoded RGB values that use the same primaries as the luminance weights.

You’re right that using luminance does not produce a perfect greyscale because there is no such thing as a perfect greyscale. But it the luminance approach is self-consistent, grounded in CIE colorimetry, and is what modern tooling typically does, like the RAW photo filter’s saturation control in Adobe Photoshop, for example.

Another point is that Godot should be self-consistent. The current PR produces different results when placing the EXR version as a Sprite vs. the PNG version as a Sprite when using this luminance remap, even though the sprite looks the same when using non-remapped colour. So this is another reason that conditional checking based on encoding is needed to correctly interpret the colour.

@allenwp

The current PR produces different results when placing the EXR version as a Sprite vs. the PNG version as a Sprite when using this luminance remap, even though the sprite looks the same when using non-remapped colour. So this is another reason that conditional checking based on encoding is needed to correctly interpret the colour.

I wholeheartedly agree. I weren't in any way trying to dispute having luminance calc done the proper way, I think we both agree that it should be consistent, that applying linear luminance dot product on non-linear color vector is wrong and that in general non-trivial linear color transforms shouldn't be applied to sRGB values. Even me mentioning Rec. 601 was just for the sake of argument that all those desaturate options that Krita provides are "greyscale" in some way. I was mostly responding to the earlier argument of "which way of getting the values is the best to use here for this feature", i.e. https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/120222#issuecomment-4693250019 etc. I'd say that this example graphic you provided is indeed the proof that going with luminance is the way producing most reasonable and least surprising result, and because Godot already uses Rec. 709 I also completely agree with using it as well. `max` is failing POLA and practical usability test IMVHO, and `avg` would basically have the same problem as luminance ATM, as using it makes sense only for linear values so switching to it wouldn't make anything simpler or better in any way - so, tl;dr I'd say that `get_luminance` after linearization is still IMO the best possible solution here in general.

I'll try fixing the code today or tomorrow, some RL stuff is brewing but I should have enough time for that I think.

Thanks for sharing your thoughts! Good to hear we’re in agreement.

I know you’ve already put a fair bit of thought into this, but I should reiterate the expectations with a new, although very small, feature: we really do need some others to chime in with their need for this before we consider merging it in. It may take months to get this feedback. Because this is something that can be done with external art tools, it’s in Godot’s interest to leave this to these external tools to reduce the number of possible bugs and complexity of maintaining. (Examples of the maintenance burden: we may need to revisit this when different file formats are added or when different colour primaries are used.)
